questions.title: Does the 'relaxed' standing standard for procedural injuries eliminate the requirement to prove concrete injury in fact?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the distinction between procedural rights and substantive injuries in Article III standing. The opinion mentions that for procedural injuries, courts 'relax' the requirements for imminence and redressability, but explicitly states they do not relax the requirement for 'injury in fact.' Does this mean a plaintiff can still sue solely because a statute granted them a procedure (like an investigation), even if they suffer no actual harm from the outcome? Or is there always a threshold requirement to show that the procedure protects some underlying concrete interest that was actually threatened?

questions.title: How does Heckler v. Chaney prevent a plaintiff from establishing causation when seeking to compel an agency investigation?
questions.question_body: The court rejected AFL's argument that OSC's failure to investigate caused their inability to get documents from DOJ. The opinion cites *Heckler v. Chaney* regarding enforcement discretion. My confusion lies in the causal chain: If OSC *must* investigate under § 1216, doesn't forcing that investigation break the chain of speculation? Why isn't it enough to say, 'If OSC investigates, they might find a violation,' rather than requiring proof that OSC will definitely force DOJ to release records? How does *Chaney* apply here if the statute allegedly makes the investigation mandatory rather than discretionary?

questions.title: Can a statutory grant of authority to investigate create an 'informational injury' if no specific right to receive data exists?
questions.question_body: AFL tried to argue they had standing because they were denied access to the 'fruits' of an OSC investigation (notices and updates). The court said § 1216 doesn't entitle anyone to receive information unless § 1214's notice requirements are applied, which seems discretionary. If Congress gives an agency power to investigate, does that automatically create a private right for citizens to know what happens during that investigation? Or is 'informational standing' strictly limited to statutes that explicitly say 'X person shall receive Y document'?

questions.title: Why did the D.C. Circuit treat the MSPB's potential future actions as an intervening cause breaking causation?
questions.question_body: In analyzing redressability, the court noted that even if OSC investigated and found a violation, they would have to go before the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), which might then sanction employees, who might then release records. The court called this too speculative because it relies on choices by independent actors (MSPB and DOJ). Isn't this true of almost every administrative enforcement scheme? Why is this specific chain considered too attenuated compared to other cases where courts order agencies to take steps knowing downstream effects depend on third parties?

questions.title: What is the practical difference between dismissing for failure to state a claim versus dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction here?
questions.question_body: The district court originally dismissed AFL's case for failing to state a claim on the merits after finding OSC made a legal error but acted within its discretion. On appeal, however, the D.C. Circuit reversed and dismissed based on Article III standing (lack of subject-matter jurisdiction). Since both result in dismissal without reaching the ultimate merits of whether DOJ violated FOIA policies, why is distinguishing between these two grounds critical? Specifically, how does characterizing this as a jurisdictional issue change how lower courts must handle similar cases in the future?

questions.title: Does § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) limit OSC's broader mandate under § 1216(a)(3)?
questions.question_body: The facts mention a split in interpretation: OSC claimed it couldn't investigate unless specific FOIA court predicates were met (§ 552), while AFL argued § 1216 gave them independent authority regardless of those predicates. Although the appellate court didn't reach this statutory interpretation issue due to standing concerns, how should I read these two sections together? Is § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) meant to be an exhaustive list of triggers for OSC involvement in FOIA matters, or just one pathway among many created by § 1216?
